speaker: johncaulfield
text: Thank you, Mayor. Good evening, council. Some updates. I think as you're aware, this weekend, we had two very peaceful demonstrations and marches here in Lakewood, one on Saturday and the other on Sunday. We haven't made aware that there is going to be another one on this Wednesday at noon, beginning at Fort Steilacoom Park. We are working to reach out to the organizer to try and get an understanding of what is planned so that we can provide any level of assistance that they may need in support of their event. So I just wanted to make you aware of that. You know, on Friday, the State Department of Health did approve Pierce County to move to phase two of Safe Start. So we are now allowed to operate under that level. It does include certain restrictions. For example, restaurants can only be at 50% capacity and certain retail stores at 30% capacity. And there's kind of a laundry list of items there. It also allows, you know, salons and barbers and other personal grooming services to open. In support of that, earlier today, we did send out some information as well as sharing it and posting it on our homepage of the city's homepage, as well as our COVID-19 webpage. Some information that the Tacoma Pierce County EDB and the Tacoma Pierce County Chamber of Commerce has put together as it relates to resources for businesses to assist them as they are allowed to reopen. I think earlier, I think our economic development manager, Becky Newton mentioned the distribution of personal protection equipment. So to businesses, actually very, very timely. That occurred on Thursday. And I wanna thank Dr. Joyce Loveday at the Clover Park Technical College for making her facility or her grounds available to do this. And we had about 550 businesses that actually came through, you know, and just in time to take advantage of that. And it was a great partnership between our team here at the city and Pierce County, as well as again, Clover Park Technical College to be able to accommodate that. Also last week, some not so positive news. We received an update from Phillips Publishing. They do our Connections Magazine, and they informed us that because of COVID-19 and the economic impacts, they are not gonna be able to continue as a viable business beyond, I think it's July or so. However, they are going to complete our Summer Connections Magazine, which is currently in the process of being prepared and will be sent out on or about June 30th. So with that, what we plan on doing is moving forward with an RFP for printing and publishing services. And we're gonna get that underway here in the next week or two. Also relating to COVID-19 and the CARES Act. So the Congress appropriated $1.5 billion to the Economic Development Administration, which is an arm of the federal government to provide support for infrastructure projects. And the Seattle region, which includes Washington State, as well as some other states here in the Pacific Northwest, has been allocated $266 million. So our team here at the city has had some conversations with personnel from EDA, as they're known as, to talk about eligible infrastructure projects. There is a two-year window in terms of when the monies need to be spent once awarded. Kind of the sweet spot for projects, the advice that we have been provided is between one and a half and $3 million. And so right now, our Public Works Engineering Department, as well as our Economic Development team are looking at a number of projects, including 146th over in Woodbrook. We just received some design monies from the Port of Tacoma to do that, as well as looking at perhaps some downtown sub-area projects. For example, the traffic intersection at Alfreda and Gravely Lake Drive. Another is the traffic signal at Steilacoom and Durango, which again, we received some design monies a number of years ago from Port of Tacoma to design. So applying for construction monies through this program might be worth the opportunity. So those are just some examples. There's a number of other projects we're looking at, but the good news is that there could be some infrastructure improvement dollars that come down here through the City of Lakewood. So more to follow on that. Also traditionally, the match has been 50-50. However, the EDA has commented that based on the ability of municipalities to pay, they would be willing to go to 80-20, where we come up with a 20% match, or even 100% with no match. And they recognize the challenges that local governments are currently facing. Also in the realm of infrastructure improvements, Public Works Engineering was alerted that the state is now taking applications for Safe Routes to School grants. And so we've identified three that we think will compete fairly effectively. One is either a signal or some kind of enhanced crossing at Military and Holden in support of the Dr. Claudia Thomas Middle School. Another is in support of Lakes High School along Far West Drive and filling in some missing sidewalks along that corridor. And then 112th, between Gravely Lake Drive and Highland Avenue. Again, some sidewalk links in support of Clover Park High School. Traditionally, high schools don't rank very well, but we think given kind of the issues that we have here in our community, that they will. So more to follow on that. In addition, the state has opened up application for bike and pedestrian grants. Quite frankly, I'll just be upfront with you. I think, as you know, in the past, we haven't had much luck obtaining these grants, but we're gonna go ahead and pursue them. One is at 84th and Pine for an enhanced crosswalk, as well as sidewalks on the north side of Silicon Boulevard between 83rd and 87th, as well as sidewalks on South Tacoma Way between 88th and 80th, which is the last link of South Tacoma Way. So we're gonna continue to evaluate those and see how they apply up to the criteria that the state has, and we'll certainly keep you posted on that. I think, as I mentioned last week, I believe that through the PSRC transportation funding process, unfortunately, we did not rank well enough to gain funding and support of our roadway projects, particularly South Tacoma Way between 88th and 80th, as well as Silicon Boulevard, the next phase of Silicon Boulevard, from Weller to 87th or 83rd. I can't remember off the top of my head what that range was. However, we did rank very high on two preservation projects. However, we're only gonna get funding for one of them, which is going to be South Tacoma Way between 96th and Silicon Boulevard. One of the questions Mr. Busich and I have had looking at who's been awarded funding, not just this cycle, but going back the last five or six cycles, why are some cities seeming to get a lot of money? And by the way, we need to be careful because in 2014, the city of Lakewood, we received almost $6 million across, I think it was five or six projects. But at the same time, there are a couple of smaller cities that seem to consistently receive funding. And one of the things that we have asked for is to look at the rating sheets in terms of how the scores are calculated. That's never been disclosed. And we would just, in terms of full transparency, we would like to see that. Mr. Busich is working with the staff at Pierce County as well as his colleagues in the other cities to try and get an understanding of that. This might be a topic of conversation for the elected officials at PCRC, which would be Council Member Farmer and Council Member Boke, if I recall. And Mr. Busich and I might wanna schedule some time to talk with you about this here in the near future. At the end of the day, it's the staff team that pulls this together. They kind of create their own rules. And they're good ones, don't get me wrong. But at the same time, we feel, and some other cities have mentioned this as well, that there seems to be a bit of an inequity across the board in terms of the allocation of funding and support of roadway projects. So again, more to come on that. May have mentioned, you may have heard me mention a couple of, about a month or two ago, that we had applied for some risk mitigation grants through WCIA, one for a speed radar and the other for a sidewalk grinder. While I'm pleased to announce that they did award funding to the city for us to be able to go out and purchase a sidewalk grinder. And those become very effective. We have sidewalk panels are pushed up because of routes and things along those lines. So we're gonna go ahead and proceed with that acquisition. We did not get funding for the speed radar. We didn't expect to get funding for both, but one or the other. But again, this is another great program that WCIA has for its members. Also the reason that the city of Lakewood for a number of years did not receive funding for this program is because I served on the executive committee for a number of years, including being president up until a couple of years ago. And so if you're on the executive committee, your city doesn't get mitigation grant funds because that's the group that makes the decision. But now that I'm off, we can apply. So we applied and I wanna thank Mr. Busich and Ms. Dodsworth actually as well for us spearheading this. And the grant is $12,000. I think as you're aware, Western State Hospital is moving forward with their facilities master plan. They have submitted it to the city. We have deemed it complete. The city of Lakewood, we are the lead SEPA agency on this. And the state is okay with us at this point in time doing that. The proposal, kind of at the 10,000 foot level, the proposal is for Western State Hospital to build a 350 bed forensics hospital on the property. That is gonna require the demolition of several existing buildings on site. It also includes building an 18 bed residential cottage at the Child Study and Treatment Center, which is over off toward 87th, as well as a new community residential treatment facility or RTF of 48 beds as well. Right now, the goal of Western State Hospital is to transition to primarily a forensics facility, meaning their civil commitment patients would over time be moved off of Western State Hospital. And right now, the majority of the 800 beds down there are civil commitment to other places throughout the state. Now, when that's gonna occur, we do not know. But again, they are moving forward with this. And given that the city is the lead SEPA agency, we have opened up the public comment period. There's a 30 day notice of application comment period that is gonna begin this Wednesday, June 10th, and will run through Friday, July 10th. We're sending out 750 notices to the surrounding property owners, and that's gonna occur here in the next day or two. We're also sending notices to all Lakewood Neighborhood Associations, multiple outside public agencies, both inside and outside the city, special interests and advocacy groups, also regional planning agencies such as the Pierce County Regional Council, South Sound Cities Association, Thurston Regional Planning Committee, and PSRC and organizations like that. Also, we learned that the TNT is looking at running a story this week to coincide with the city's public comment notice. And Mr. Buehrer was essentially talked with the TNT late last week about what's going on down there. I'm sure they talked with Western State Hospital and our DSHS as well. And I know they had asked to speak with Mayor Anderson, and I believe the mayor is looking to speak with the reporter here in the next day or two. The city, we have also created a standalone website called wshmasterplan.org, which will go live this Thursday, or there's about, and it'll be, again, an opportunity for people to come and see all the material specific to the master planning process, as well as comments and feedbacks, and just be able to participate in the process as well. And down at Fort Steilacoom Park, so the barn that, if you're looking at the H barn, there's a barn off of the back to the left. It's an older barn. It's not used for anything or storage. It's empty. Earlier today, a tree fell on it and crushed it, or crushed a good portion of it. And so we're gonna secure the site if it hasn't already been done, post no trespassing, things along those lines. Obviously, there's no way to rebuild that. And so similar to the barn that came down next to it, you might recall back in, I think it was 2015 or 16, we'll now move forward with abating that, and that's gonna require us to go through a fairly detailed process with the state of Washington to take that down. Lastly, wanted to make the council aware that tomorrow, myself, our senior policy analyst, Shannon Kelly-Fong, and our state government relations team is going to meet with state representative Jake Fye, who is chair of the House Transportation Committee. The purpose of meeting with him is twofold. The first, to provide him an update on our Lakewood Landing project, as well as our desire to relocate the Washtop Maintenance Facility and the importance of LRF, Local Revitalization Financing, and or TIF, to be able to move that to allow for development within that area. And it's an opportunity for him to learn more about the project. The second purpose of the meeting is to hear from him as chair of the Transportation Committee, a project that he is spearheading, which actually is a very good one. And that is to add an HOV lane, to continue an HOV lane from 38th and Tacoma, all the way down to Thorn Lane. Now that, we would like to see that go all the way down to the Nisqually Bridge, and then of course, points south over the bridge. But in any event, our purpose tomorrow is to listen to the representative and get an understanding of what the proposal is. We do understand that he is not looking to do the, what I would call the, just painting, which would be kind of, you might recall in 2017, Washtop prepared a study for this corridor that identified several options. The real simple option, if you will, was to essentially put down paint and squeeze in five lanes where there's four. We understand that representative Fye desire is to go with really the better option, which is to construct a brand new lane, which would result in a number of interchange improvements that would be required, including at Bridgeport and Gravely Lake Drive, as well as a number of bridges that probably would have to be addressed. And in Lakewood, that would be South Tacoma Way, 47th and New York Avenue bridges. So again, our purpose tomorrow is to learn more about what his proposal is and what his idea is. And I'm sure he's gonna want at some time in the future, our feedback on that. So again, just wanted to give you a heads up on that, and I'll be more than happy to report out on what happened at that meeting next week. So with that council, that's my report. Thank you.
